about.title: curiosity came before the career.
about.lead: my relationship with technology started by watching my uncle work with computer maintenance and radio internet. before I knew how to program, I already liked opening things up, installing, modifying and trying to understand how they worked.
about.context: as a teenager, that curiosity moved through operating systems, video editing and the web. I started projects before I knew how to finish them and gradually learned HTML, CSS, JavaScript and PHP by experimenting, taking courses and documenting some of the work publicly.
about.description: at IFRO, informal learning met teachers, fundamentals and larger projects. the path was not linear: formal study sometimes meant revisiting things I had already encountered while opening access to domains, people and responsibilities I would not have reached alone.
about.storyTitle: from experiments to software people depend on.
about.story:
computers were part of my life before software development was. my uncle worked with computer maintenance and radio internet, installed the internet at home, fixed our machines and encouraged me to study technology. the same curiosity also existed away from the screen: I liked taking things apart, experimenting with speakers and batteries and trying to understand how they worked internally.

between roughly 2017 and 2020 I learned mostly by experimenting. I moved between Windows and Linux, video editing and web development, built projects beyond what I knew how to finish and later started documenting part of that process on JipaCoding. courses from Origamid and programming/logic practice helped organize some of the scattered learning. in 2019 I was already sending patches to third-party open-source projects; merged work from that period includes pwa-icon-generator, extenso.js and Vue-related projects.

I entered IFRO's technical program in informatics in 2021 already familiar with programming and Linux. formal study did not simply move me forward in a straight line: I revisited fundamentals, used C# in the first programming/logic classes and adjusted tools and operating systems to the coursework. more importantly, the institute added teachers, teamwork and institutional projects. in PROINFE's early phase I studied NestJS and Keycloak and participated in meetings and analysis before there was much implementation, which taught me that software work begins before a codebase is ready to receive features.

in 2022 I worked full stack on an institutional surveys platform and built the IFRO schedule viewer that evolved from cropping a large PDF to extracting and normalizing its data. the viewer led me toward SISGHA/Ladesa in 2023, where the problem moved from consuming an already-published timetable to the academic entities and constraints involved in producing one. web scraping followed another connected path: public-page experiments became AVA Pro's authenticated Moodle integration and later a paid four-source catalog-ingestion job. a merged Nuxt Auth fix from 2023 is another example of the kind of boundary that interests me: client navigation and SSR reached the same code through different asynchronous behavior.

from 2024 onward, more of my work lived in software that already had users and operational consequences. central de vagas reached production and brought maintenance, support and training into my routine. freelance work put me inside inherited PHP software during a team transition and in an end-to-end WordPress delivery. Ladesa contributions crossed application code, scheduling rules, Kubernetes/ingress work and later domain/API, authentication, resilience and calendar changes. in 2025 and 2026 I also worked on internal production systems at a private company.

today I continue working on applications and open source while studying Go and infrastructure more deliberately. a homelab and public engineering notebook give me room to investigate networking, virtualization, containers, identity, orchestration and observability. I do not see that as leaving software development for another field: the recurring interest is how independent systems communicate, how information moves between them and what is hidden below the interfaces we normally use. some of those investigations become products, some become libraries or articles, and some remain experiments. I prefer keeping those differences visible instead of rewriting the trajectory as if every attempt had been a finished success.

projects.name: Meu Caderno
projects.purpose: an early-stage open-source local-first study application for organizing subjects, courses, learning projects, activities, grades, attendance, materials and accumulated knowledge without making a server mandatory.
projects.body:
Meu Caderno is an early-stage personal project where product decisions and software architecture meet. the project is designed around offline-first use, user-owned local data, optional synchronization, progressive disclosure and avoiding lock-in. a project constitution makes those principles explicit, including reversibility, consent and limits around automated or AI-assisted behavior.

the current codebase is a Bun/Nx monorepo. the UI-independent core already contains typed domain models and Zod schemas for contexts, profiles, library, notebooks, activities and federation, alongside persistence/federation structures and adapters; the application is a Nuxt/Vue PWA designed to run without a mandatory backend. the delivery pipeline also reflects the same concern for control and verifiability, with GitHub Pages deployment, CodeQL, dependency automation, workflow linting/security checks and build attestations. the application is still at MVP/early-development stage, so this record remains hidden from the public project selection until the product surface is substantial enough to represent completed work rather than architectural direction.

this is not the first time local data and user control appeared in one of my projects. Ya Time Marker, a small PWA I published in 2021, already kept its usage history on the device and explicitly supported importing, exporting and deleting the user's data without collecting it centrally. I do not treat the two applications as one continuous architecture, but the older project makes the current local-first principles less disconnected from the rest of my history: the vocabulary became more deliberate; the concern itself is older.

projects.name: ANP historical data
projects.purpose: a Go validation project for collecting, reading and normalizing public historical fuel-price data from ANP/gov.br sources.
projects.body: this repository is still small and does not have the documentation or product surface I would require before presenting it as a finished CLI. its value in the portfolio is narrower: it records part of my current Go study through a concrete data-ingestion problem, with code separated around source access, reading and normalization. I keep it hidden for now rather than describing an unfinished validation as a published tool.

projects.name: AVA Pro
projects.purpose: a browser extension for Moodle platforms with enrolled-course listing/search, pinned courses, automatic-login flows, chat access and background checks for new messages.
projects.body:
this project entry describes the artifact itself. AVA Pro packaged several Moodle-facing features into a web extension built around TypeScript/React: course navigation, course pinning, access/login helpers and chat/message flows that could be reached from the browser extension rather than only from the Moodle pages.

the repository is archival and I do not present it as an extension that should be installed against current Moodle/browser versions. the separate case study carries the more useful historical story: how the project moved my scraping experiments from static DOM extraction toward authenticated application flows, while this page remains the concise record of what was actually built.

projects.name: home lab
projects.purpose: an ongoing personal infrastructure lab where I investigate the layers around an application in practice: virtual machines, segmented networks, VPNs, firewalls, containers, Kubernetes, identity and observability.
projects.status: investigation · ongoing · repository content to update
projects.body: this entry is intentionally kept as a CMS draft for now. the current lab has evolved beyond what the older public repository documents, and I do not want the portfolio to imply that the repository is a complete or reproducible description of the current environment. the public infrastructure & cluster notebook documents individual investigations more accurately while this broader lab record catches up.

projects.name: infrastructure & cluster notebook
projects.purpose: a public engineering notebook where I record infrastructure and cluster investigations through hypotheses, reproducible tests, failures and revisions instead of presenting the material as a finished tutorial.
projects.problem: infrastructure learning easily turns into disconnected commands or configuration snippets. I wanted a record that preserves what I was trying to verify, the environment in which I tested it and what changed when an assumption failed.
projects.current_focus: networking, containers, K3s/Kubernetes and the operational layers around self-hosted services.
projects.body: this is deliberately a notebook rather than a finished architecture, but it has an inspectable and reproducible technical surface: hypotheses, configurations, tests, failures and revisions around the current infrastructure lab. it remains visible because the artifact itself is the engineering record, not a promise of a future product.

projects.name: JipaCoding
projects.purpose: a public video archive that preserves different phases of my technical learning, from early PHP/CSS/JavaScript experiments to algorithms, image generation, browser extensions, automation and infrastructure.
projects.body: JipaCoding remains useful as longitudinal evidence and as a source that connects several historical artifacts, but it is not itself a software project. under the current maturity and classification rule it stays in the CMS/editorial inventory instead of occupying a slot in the public selected-project list.

projects.name: Fantastic Images
projects.purpose: an older TypeScript/Fabric.js exploration for describing image templates and rendering generated compositions on canvas.
projects.body: Fantastic Images grew out of a broader line of template-editor experiments, including a Fabric.js core, Vue/PWA and later React editor work, node-oriented paths and the later `@fantastic-images/*` packages. it remains useful as development history and as context for the later, narrower `fabricjs-object-fit` library. under the current maturity rule, however, the broad exploration itself stays out of the public selected-project list.

projects.name: parcel-resolver-pnpm
projects.purpose: a 2021 proof-of-concept Parcel resolver that investigated the way Parcel treated pnpm's symlinked dependencies as source dependencies.
projects.body: the resolver was intentionally a small validation tied to Parcel internals of that period. it explored recognizing packages coming from node_modules/.pnpm and restoring dependency semantics when symlinked dependencies were treated as source dependencies. the investigation remains useful as technical history and supports the related writing, but it is not a finished resolver I would recommend today, so it stays out of the public selected-project list.

projects.name: Friendly TNSVue
projects.purpose: a 2019 proof of concept for automating parts of the migration from Vue projects to NativeScript-Vue through a CLI, migration service and reusable migration models.
projects.body:
Friendly TNSVue was an early experiment in treating source migration as a programmable transformation rather than a manual rewrite. the archived v1 repository is organized as a Lerna monorepo with three published scoped packages: a CLI, a migration service and migration-model presets. the command-line flow was designed to run inside a Vue project and apply migration rules toward NativeScript-Vue.

the project was exploratory and was never a complete general-purpose migration product. its historical value is preserved in the CMS, but under the current maturity rule it stays out of the public selected-project list because it remained a proof of concept rather than a completed tool/product.

projects.name: gir-js
projects.purpose: an unfinished investigation into using GObject introspection metadata to expose native libraries to JavaScript runtimes through FFI and generate TypeScript-facing information from typelib data.
projects.problem: bindings around GLib/GObject often depend on runtime-specific integration. I wanted to understand how much of that bridge could be derived dynamically from the introspection metadata itself.
projects.current_focus: the repository is currently a research sketch rather than an active library; an earlier related POC, quickjs-gobject, explored the same boundary from QuickJS.
projects.body:
this entry is intentionally kept hidden from the public project selection while the repository remains small and incomplete. it records an idea and technical direction rather than a usable package: reading GObject introspection typelib metadata, calling native c functions dynamically through FFI/libffi and deriving TypeScript-facing information.

the subject is still useful as part of my private/editorial inventory because it records an interest in runtimes, native interfaces, metadata-driven bindings and the boundary between JavaScript and system libraries. the earlier quickjs-gobject repository is a related proof of concept, not a separate finished project.

projects.name: Unispec
projects.purpose: an archived research/POC around declaring contracts once and deriving tooling for ecosystems such as NestJS, GraphQL, OpenAPI/Swagger and QuickType.
projects.problem: I was exploring whether schema, validation, documentation and generated contracts could share a smaller source of truth instead of being repeatedly declared across frameworks.
projects.current_focus: archived. the experiment produced multiple npm packages and drivers, but it never became a stable general-purpose solution.
projects.body: Unispec grew into an Nx/pnpm workspace with AST utilities and drivers for areas such as NestJS, GraphQL, Swagger/OpenAPI and QuickType, with several packages published to npm. that implementation makes it useful historical evidence, but the work remained explicitly experimental and never became a stable general-purpose solution. under the current maturity rule it stays in the CMS as research history rather than in the public selected-project list.

projects.name: Ya Time Marker
projects.purpose: a 2021 Ionic/React PWA for marking and searching time records while keeping the user's history on the device, with import, export and deletion under the user's control.
projects.body:
Ya Time Marker is an older application, but its README makes one part of it unexpectedly relevant to my current work: official versions explicitly did not collect or report user data, stored usage/history locally and allowed the user to import, export and delete that data. the project used Ionic/React with PouchDB and was distributed as a PWA.

I was not using the current vocabulary or architecture of Meu Caderno in 2021, so I do not present Ya Time Marker as the same design carried forward unchanged. it is useful as historical evidence that local data, portability and avoiding unnecessary collection already mattered to me before I later made those principles explicit in a larger local-first project.

projects.name: Outro Bun
projects.purpose: a one-off Bun/TypeScript tool that turned a graduation-song spreadsheet export into an automated download and media-processing workflow using yt-dlp and FFmpeg.
projects.body:
Outro Bun was deliberately small and practical. it accepted a CSV exported from the graduation-song spreadsheet, used the links and optional start/end information in that data, and automated media preparation with yt-dlp and FFmpeg. the repository also contains a containerized development path around Bun and the media tools.

it remains visible because it completed a concrete workflow and has inspectable implementation; the status makes clear that it was a one-off automation rather than a maintained product.

projects.body: the public repository contains an MVP workspace with a React/TypeScript/Vite application, a generators package, a deployed demo and a JipaCoding walkthrough. it remains useful as a historical source artifact, but it is a small demonstrator rather than a substantial standalone project, so it stays out of the public selected-project list.

projects.name: Alset ALOC
projects.purpose: a C#/WPF rental-management desktop system built as a team project for completion of IFRO's technical program in informatics.
projects.body:
Alset ALOC belongs in the project archive rather than in the experiments collection. the repository README identifies it as a requirement for completion of the technical program in informatics and credits a four-person team: Vitor Daniel Silva Melo, Gabriel Rodrigues Antunes, Gabriel Lucena Ferreira and Pedro Henrique de Melo Batista. the source is a .NET/WPF desktop application with XAML views and a database/data-access layer.

the public commit history records my direct participation in the repository, but I keep the portfolio description at the team-project level instead of turning shared coursework into a personal architecture claim. its main value in the portfolio is contextual: it closes part of the formal IFRO/C# thread mentioned in my trajectory and shows why desktop coursework later pulled my development environment back toward Windows.

cases.title: central de vagas em creches
cases.summary: I worked as a scholarship developer on the team behind a public-sector platform for childcare applications, service workflows and waiting-list management. it became one of my first sustained experiences with software that reached production and continued demanding support after deployment.
cases.meta: public-sector partnership · IFRO, TCE-RO and DPR-RO · 2024–2025
cases.context: the project brought together IFRO with public institutions in Rondônia. the system had to represent different stages of service and legal and socioeconomic priority criteria while making waiting-list handling more transparent and traceable. that meant the queue was not merely an ordered list: its position depended on rules that needed to be represented consistently in the application.
cases.role: I contributed across frontend and backend, including authentication, waiting-list generation, feature development, refactoring and critical/non-critical bug fixes. I also participated in rollout, support and user training, so my work continued after a feature was merged and into the way the system was actually operated.
cases.result: the platform reached production. for me, the important shift was responsibility: requirements came from a real administrative process, changes could affect people waiting for a public service, and maintenance/support were part of the engineering work rather than something outside it.
cases.body:
central de vagas was collaborative work, not a system I designed or implemented alone. I joined the project as a scholarship developer and worked alongside other developers and the project coordination in a partnership involving IFRO, the tribunal de contas do estado de Rondônia (TCE-RO) and the defensoria pública do estado de Rondônia (DPR-RO).

the waiting-list domain made the project more than a CRUD application. eligibility and ordering had to account for administrative stages and priority criteria defined outside the software. my contribution included the code around queue generation as well as application work around authentication and the workflows that supported it.

the other important part was what happened after implementation. I worked on bugs and refactoring, supported users, participated in training and helped with rollout. that period changed my reference for a 'finished' feature: production software keeps accumulating operational context, exceptions and feedback after the initial code is done.

cases.title: IFRO Ji-Paraná schedules
cases.status: personal project used at the campus
cases.summary: I built a tool that turned the campus's weekly schedule pdfs into information students could browse by class and teacher. what began as a cropping shortcut later became structured data, a separate interface and eventually a bridge into the much harder problem of generating and managing academic schedules.
cases.context: schedules arrived as a large PDF, which made finding one class or teacher unnecessarily slow. the first version simply cropped the right region of the document from mapped coordinates. later I wanted the schedule to become actual structured data instead of remaining an image of a table.
cases.role: I evolved the project from coordinate-based cropping to PDF.js extraction and parsing. the public history later separates the work into an extractor package, a TypeScript data service backed by SQLite/TypeORM and a React application. my commits span the extractor/data repositories and the application, including weekly data updates and interface work.
cases.result: the tool gained adoption among students at the campus and became one of my first projects whose usefulness I could observe directly through other people's everyday use. it also changed the question I was asking: after improving how a finished schedule was consumed, I learned about SISGHA/Ladesa and the institutional work of producing and managing those schedules under constraints. I began contributing there in 2023.
cases.body:
the first implementation attacked the shortest path to the pain point: map the class region in the PDF and return a cropped image. that worked, but the document was still the source of truth and the application could not reason about the schedule.

the next iterations extracted text with PDF.js and normalized the unstructured table-like content. public repositories later separated extraction, a data service that persisted normalized information with SQLite, and a React/TypeScript application with MUI, React Query, virtualization and client-side search. the architecture was not the starting point; it emerged as the problem and my understanding of it grew.

that evolution exposed another boundary. displaying a published schedule was only the last step of a larger process. once I learned about SISGHA, I moved from a personal viewer into a collaborative system concerned with academic entities, scheduling rules and timetable generation itself. the two projects are therefore different in ownership and scope, but they are connected in my trajectory: horários taught me to turn an awkward document into usable data; SISGHA/Ladesa exposed the domain that existed before the PDF was generated.

cases.title: SIPEC
cases.summary: I worked full stack on an institutional surveys platform where users could create projects, assemble forms and collect responses under different access modes.
cases.context: the system modelled configurable projects, forms and questions, with authentication and different ways of controlling access to responses.
cases.role: I worked on the React/Next.js frontend using the brazilian government design system, a NestJS and PostgreSQL backend, authentication with Keycloak and the response experience with SurveyJS. responses could be configured around anonymous, authenticated and token-linked access. the public v2 history also preserves my 2023 work in form/question components and shared schemas.
cases.result: it was one of the first larger institutional systems I worked on and the project took me to the national science and technology week in Brasília in 2022. the archived v2 code records a monorepo with a Next.js application, NestJS endpoint, PostgreSQL, Keycloak and Meilisearch.
cases.body:
the available repositories preserve different stages of the project. the v1 material is split between frontend, backend/authentication and questionnaire-related repositories. the archived v2 work later brings application and endpoint services, PostgreSQL, Keycloak, Meilisearch and shared packages into a monorepo.

the v2 Git history preserves my february and march 2023 work in question components and schema declarations, despite the current GitHub repository having been republished into the organization later.

for me, the project was also a change in scale. I was working across both sides of an institutional application, dealing with authentication, configurable data structures and multiple response flows rather than a single-purpose personal tool.

cases.title: SISGHA / Ladesa: academic management and scheduling
cases.summary: I came to SISGHA after building a personal viewer for already-published schedules and realizing that displaying a timetable was only the end of a much larger scheduling problem. my contributions then crossed several phases: early academic CRUD/UI and generator rules, infrastructure and cluster maintenance, and later substantial application/domain/platform work.
cases.meta: IFRO · contributions in different phases from 2023 to 2026
cases.context: academic scheduling combines campuses, courses, classes, subjects, teachers, calendars, availability and institutional constraints. once the goal moves from displaying a finished PDF to generating and managing the schedule itself, relationships, permissions, recurrence, conflicts and optimization rules have to remain consistent across services and interfaces.
cases.role: in the early phase, merged work includes the first dashboard course-page implementation, backend CRUD/domain/authz work for academic modalities, and a timetable-generator restriction preventing a generated schedule from assigning a teacher across three shifts. I explicitly credited @procopiouriel for major help with that generator rule. in 2024–2025 I also contributed to cluster maintenance and infrastructure documentation involving Kubernetes deployments, ingress behavior, container-resource cleanup and K3s notes. in 2026 my contributions moved heavily through API/domain restructuring, transactional operations, calendar/RRule rules, resilience around dependencies, generated API clients, web authentication and the .NET timetable generator.
cases.result: the merged history documents several different ways of participating in the same long-running collaborative system: learning the academic domain, implementing application features, expressing scheduling restrictions, operating deployment infrastructure and later restructuring parts of the platform. it is not a system I authored alone; its value as a case is precisely the breadth of concrete contribution over time.
cases.body:
the connection with my personal horários project matters. that tool started from the consumption side: a large PDF was inconvenient, so I first cropped it and later extracted and normalized its data. SISGHA exposed what came before that PDF: the academic entities, availability and rules required to construct a valid timetable.

the public repository history preserves some of my early 2023 work. in the web application, a merged PR implemented the first dashboard page for courses. in management-service, another merged PR added the academic `Modalidade` model and CRUD flow across DTOs, services, rest/GraphQL presentation and authorization policies. in the timetable generator, a merged rule prevented a teacher from being scheduled across all three daily shifts; I worked on it with substantial help from @procopiouriel.

later contributions moved beyond those initial features. in 2024–2025 I worked on deployment/cluster material, including Kubernetes/ingress adjustments, cleanup of container resources and infrastructure/K3s documentation. in 2026, representative merged changes include moving rest/GraphQL presentation into corresponding core modules, restructuring API v2 operations around the academic domain, transactional batch creation and uniqueness rules for journals, calendar work with RRule recurrence and conflict/permission checks, dependency-health tracking with retry/backoff and degraded behavior, local OpenAPI client generation, a different web authentication flow and restructuring the .NET generator into clearer domain/application/infrastructure, API and worker concerns.

cases.title: fabricjs-object-fit
cases.summary: I maintain a library that brings CSS-like object-fit and object-position behavior to Fabric.js while preserving the configuration through canvas serialization.
cases.context: fitting arbitrary images into fixed canvas regions without distortion repeatedly recreates the same cover, contain and positioning logic. Fabric.js does not expose that behavior with the same abstraction developers already know from CSS.
cases.role: I designed the library API around cover, contain, fill, none and scale-down modes; implemented pixel, percentage and named-anchor positioning; integrated serialization round-trips; and maintain tests, documentation and automated checks for current Fabric.js versions.
cases.result: the package is published on npm and now targets Fabric.js v7+, with a usage guide, generated API documentation, tests and automated dependency/security checks.
cases.body: the project is also a useful continuation of earlier experiments such as Fantastic Images. the subject stayed similar (predictable image composition on a canvas), but the implementation became a smaller reusable library with a focused contract, tests, documentation and compatibility work instead of a larger template-generation system.

cases.title: AVA Pro: Moodle inside a browser extension
cases.summary: AVA Pro grew from my web-scraping experiments into a browser extension that interacted with Moodle as an authenticated application: courses, search and pinning, login flows, chats and background checks for new messages.
cases.meta: web extensions · authenticated web application integration · 2021–2022
cases.context: my earlier scraping experiments mostly dealt with information already present in HTML. Moodle was more interesting because useful information belonged to an authenticated application with its own requests, sessions and dynamic flows. the goal was not to copy a page into an extension; it was to make selected parts of the learning environment usable from the browser UI.
cases.role: I built the extension and explored how to obtain and present Moodle data across static page content and application-driven flows. the resulting project surfaced enrolled courses, supported search and pinned courses, automated parts of login, exposed chat browsing/conversation and checked for new messages in the background.
cases.result: the repository stopped active development in 2022, so I treat it as an archive rather than a maintained Moodle product. it remains one of the personal projects I value most because it changed how I thought about web automation: from selecting DOM nodes to understanding a running application, its authenticated state and the information exchanged between its parts.
cases.body:
AVA Pro sits in the middle of a longer learning path. a simple browser-scraping demonstration first showed me that a page could be treated as a data source. I later recorded my own scraping experiment with public IFPR notices. those examples were largely static: the information I wanted was already in the document.

Moodle pushed the idea further. courses, login state, conversations and new messages are not just a static document. building them into an extension required me to treat the website as an application and understand where its information came from and how authenticated flows behaved. the extension could list and search enrolled courses, keep selected courses pinned, automate parts of access, browse and send chat messages and perform background checks for new messages.

cases.title: Scrap Rain: multi-source product catalog scraping
cases.summary: I built Scrap Rain for a freelance job that collected product catalogs from four furniture websites and turned different page structures into data that could be persisted and updated incrementally.
cases.context: the four sources exposed similar business information through different HTML structures. the extraction had to collect product names, descriptions, images and characteristics and support repeated executions without treating every run as a full import from scratch.
cases.role: I implemented the scraping and persistence flow. records were processed incrementally instead of keeping the entire catalog in memory, and previously stored data was compared so later runs could persist new or changed information without creating duplicate records.
cases.result: this was one of the first times a subject I had been studying through browser scraping became paid work with practical concerns around multiple sources, memory use, persistence and repeat execution. I keep the client identity out of the public portfolio.
cases.body:
Scrap Rain is the same work I had previously described only as the anonymous four-site furniture scraping freelance, not a separate experiment. giving the case its real project name avoids keeping two identities for the same work.

its technical significance is also clearer when placed next to the earlier scraping history rather than treated as an isolated scraper. static page experiments taught me how to extract repeated structures; AVA Pro added authenticated application flows; Scrap Rain added data-volume, persistence and repeated-run concerns. the separate scraping retrospective carries that longer learning path, while this case stays focused on the paid delivery itself.

the exact period I am comfortable publishing still needs confirmation, so the case remains hidden even though the underlying work is now consolidated under one canonical identity.

writings.title: before I knew how to program, I already wanted to understand computers
writings.excerpt: radio internet, Windows installation media, broken customizations, Linux distributions, XAMPP and projects I had no idea how to finish: the part of my technology story that came before formal training.
writings.body:
my first references in technology did not come from a programming course. they came from watching my uncle work with computer maintenance and radio internet. he installed the internet at home, formatted our computers, brought CDs and USB drives with Windows installation media and games, and was the person who kept telling me that learning technology and programming could be worth pursuing. sometimes the work was as tangible as climbing an internet tower; other times it was sitting in front of a machine trying to make it work again.

computers were also simply where I played. Habbo, browser games, Second Life and later Minecraft were part of the attraction. I wanted to record Minecraft videos with friends and cousins and experimented with video editing before I had any professional reason to do so. away from the computer I liked the same kind of exploration: taking toy cars apart, connecting speakers and batteries, trying to repair things and seeing what was inside them.

around 2017 and 2018 I started deliberately looking for more technical things. one of the detours was downloading Kali Linux because the idea of hacking Wi-Fi sounded exciting. I did not pursue that, but it was part of my first contact with Linux. at the same time I was modifying Windows 8 and Windows 10 to look different, sometimes trying to imitate macOS or Linux desktops. eventually I broke a Windows installation badly enough that moving to Linux stopped being only an aesthetic experiment.

then came the distribution-hopping phase: Deepin, elementary OS, Fedora, Ubuntu, Zorin, Linux Mint and others. what mattered was not finding the perfect distribution. it was discovering that the operating system itself was something I could replace, inspect and configure instead of accepting as a fixed part of the computer.

the web entered through HTML, CSS, JavaScript and PHP. I used XAMPP and WAMP, followed YouTube tutorials about database connections and WordPress and downloaded source code I barely understood. at different points I tried to run my own Habbo-like server or other web applications locally simply by reproducing instructions. that kind of learning had obvious limits, but it gave me an environment where changing a file immediately changed something I could see.

I also tried to create a social network called UAS. I did not have the knowledge or resources to make it into a real product, but the ambition was useful: I was already trying to put authentication, pages, data and users together before I had a good mental model for the pieces. many of my early projects were like that: larger than my ability to finish them.

Origamid courses around that period helped organize some of what had been scattered experimentation. web design, frontend, WordPress and even the tooling around npm gave names and structure to things I had been discovering through tutorials. SoloLearn served another role: before IFRO I would practice programming and logic challenges from my phone.

I later started publishing some of these experiments on JipaCoding. looking back at the public videos is unusual because they preserve versions of my technical thinking that I would never reconstruct accurately from memory: custom form controls, PHP and reCAPTCHA, CSS object-fit, JavaScript algorithms, Minesweeper and flood filling, image manipulation, Vue and NativeScript, browser extensions and web scraping.

none of this forms a clean curriculum. I jumped between operating systems, web development, graphics, video and small projects, often without knowing enough to understand the whole stack. formal training at IFRO later made me revisit fundamentals I had partially encountered already. the useful part of that non-linear path was not being 'ahead'; it was arriving with a habit of experimenting and then having teachers, projects and theory help turn that habit into something more deliberate.

before.excerpt: radio internet, Windows installation media, broken customizations, Linux distributions, XAMPP and projects I had no idea how to finish: the part of my technology story that came before formal training.

computers were also simply where I played. Habbo, browser games, Second Life and later Minecraft were part of the attraction. writings.title: when a personal portfolio becomes an engineering laboratory
writings.excerpt: a personal site gave me a low-risk place to experiment with content architecture, reproducible toolchains, LaTeX, browser checks, security scanning, CI trade-offs and deployment, including learning when to remove complexity again.
writings.body:
a personal portfolio is small enough that it does not need the operational machinery of a large product. that is exactly why mine became a useful engineering laboratory: I could try tooling and quality practices in a repository I controlled, observe the cost of each choice and later remove what did not justify its weight.

the repository grew beyond a single Next.js application. content lives separately from rendering concerns and is edited through TinaCMS; the résumé is another output of the same broader content system and has a LaTeX/PDF path; development tooling is intended to be reproducible rather than depending entirely on whatever happens to be installed on my machine. that structure forced me to think about boundaries that do not appear in a one-page static site: which data should be shared, which artifacts are generated, and which tools belong to development rather than production.

CI became another experiment. at different points I added linting and formatting, type checks, dead-code/duplication/complexity checks, browser tests, accessibility and Lighthouse checks, dependency and security scanners, secret detection and workflow validation. the useful lesson was not 'more checks is always better'. running every heavy check on every deployment made the feedback loop slower and created infrastructure work that was disproportionate to an MVP. the current direction separates fast confidence from heavier scheduled or deliberate validation and keeps Vercel focused on deployment rather than making a personal site simulate a large release platform.

toolchain reliability produced its own problems. building the résumé required TeX tooling; repeatedly downloading binaries in CI eventually ran into rate limiting, which pushed me to think about Hermit/Tectonic caches, cache poisoning, trust boundaries and whether a cache was actually worth introducing. deployment also exposed permission boundaries: instead of broadening a Vercel token just to make `vercel pull` happy, I preferred a project-scoped token and adjusted the workflow around what that credential should legitimately be able to do.

the site therefore records two kinds of work at once. the visible result is intentionally simple: pages, projects, cases, writing and a résumé. behind it, the repository is where I can investigate build systems, containers, CI, browser automation, accessibility, security and content modelling without claiming that every experiment belongs in the final architecture. the most useful changes are sometimes removals: deciding that an OCI image, a heavy CD test matrix or another abstraction does not yet pay for itself.

toolchain reliability produced its own problems. building the résumé required TeX tooling; repeatedly downloading binaries in CI eventually ran into rate limiting, which pushed me to think about Hermit/Tectonic caches, cache poisoning, trust boundaries and whether a cache was actually worth introducing. deployment also exposed permission boundaries: instead of broadening a Vercel token just to make `vercel pull` happy, I preferred a project-scoped token and adjusted the workflow around what that credential should legitimately be able to do.

writings.title: AI changed how I develop software, not why I care about it
writings.excerpt: I learned to program before generative AI was part of the workflow. today I use it heavily, but I still see architecture, constraints, business rules and quality criteria as engineering decisions rather than prompts.
writings.body:
I learned programming in a period when getting a small application working usually meant spending much more time reading documentation, following tutorials, doing logic exercises and debugging without a model generating the next implementation for me. I do not think that makes the old process morally better, but it shaped how I relate to code: I had to build enough internal references to notice when something did not make sense.

generative AI is now an unavoidable and very useful part of my workflow. I use it for research, debugging, comparing approaches, understanding unfamiliar systems and implementing code. used well, it can compress hours of mechanical work and make it practical to explore areas that would otherwise take much longer to enter.

the part I do not want to outsource is judgment. a model can generate an architecture, but it does not own the cost of operating it. it can implement a rule, but it does not decide whether the rule represents the business correctly. it can produce tests, abstractions and infrastructure, but someone still has to define what quality means for that system and verify the result.

for me, using AI well means giving it constraints rather than asking it to replace them: the architecture I am aiming for, the security model, the cost I can accept, the rules the system must preserve and the trade-offs I am willing to make. the more capable the tool becomes, the more useful it is to know what I want from it and why.

that is also why I do not want to build a professional identity around being a person who writes code faster than AI. software was interesting to me before code generation became cheap because I liked systems, information, automation and understanding how things connected. those interests survive changes in the way code itself is produced.

writings.title: from cropping a schedule PDF to turning it into data
writings.excerpt: a retrospective on how the IFRO schedule viewer evolved from fixed image coordinates to PDF.js extraction, normalization and a queryable web interface.
writings.body:
in 2022, the weekly schedules at IFRO Ji-Paraná arrived as a large PDF. the information was there, but finding one class inside the document was inconvenient enough that I built a tool for it.

the first version did not try to understand the PDF. I mapped where each class appeared on the page, converted the document to an image and cropped the correct rectangle. the user selected a course and class and got only the part of the schedule that mattered. it was crude, but it worked, and that made it a useful first version.

the limitation was obvious: coordinates are not data. if the document changed its layout, the assumptions could break, and I still could not ask questions such as which teacher had a class at a given time. I then moved to PDF.js and started extracting the text layer instead.

that created a different problem. a table that is visually obvious to a person does not necessarily arrive as rows and columns when text is extracted from a PDF. I had to reconstruct structure from fragments, normalize the values and turn the document into JSON. Lodash helped with part of that transformation, but most of the work was understanding the recurring shape of the source and encoding those rules explicitly.

once the schedule was structured data, the frontend could stop thinking in rectangles. I built a SPA that could browse schedules by class and teacher, show which class was active at the current time and consume the normalized JSON without depending on the original PDF during normal use. I also wanted it to remain useful with limited connectivity, which pushed the interface toward an offline-friendly model.

the interesting part of this project was not replacing one library with another. it was the sequence of representations: first I treated the PDF as an image, then as extracted text, then as a domain-specific data source. each version attacked the same everyday problem at a different level, and the simpler first attempt gave me enough feedback to justify the harder one.

that progression eventually exposed the limit of the project itself. the viewer began after a schedule already existed. learning about SISGHA/Ladesa showed me the domain on the other side of the PDF: courses, classes, teachers, availability, calendars and constraints that have to be reconciled before a timetable can be published at all. I started contributing there in 2023. the personal viewer and the collaborative scheduling system are separate projects, but this is the point where one led naturally into the other.

writings.title: from querySelector to data pipelines: how scraping changed for me
writings.excerpt: a browser-DOM demonstration led to public-notice scraping, then to an authenticated Moodle extension and finally to a paid four-source catalog-ingestion project.
writings.body:

writings.title: RRule is the recurrence syntax, not the calendar domain
writings.excerpt: implementing recurring academic-calendar events meant deciding how dates are normalized, occurrences are expanded, durations are preserved, invalid rules degrade and unbounded recurrence is contained.
writings.body:
I used RRule in Ladesa while working on calendar scheduling and occurrence queries. the library solved an important part of the problem (parsing and expanding a recurrence rule), but the pull request made the boundary clear: a recurrence specification does not decide how the rest of an application's calendar should behave.

the query receives a date range and persisted schedule items. non-repeating items can pass through directly; repeating items have to be expanded into occurrences inside that range. the implementation normalizes date-only strings to explicit midnight UTC before expansion, because allowing the runtime to interpret an underspecified date implicitly makes timezone behavior part of the bug surface. for each occurrence, the original event duration is preserved by calculating the difference between the stored start and end and applying it to the generated start date.

recurrence also needs containment. an RRULE can describe a very large or effectively unbounded sequence, while an API request needs a finite amount of work. the implementation therefore limits expansion to 1,000 occurrences per schedule item in one query and emits a warning when the generated set is larger. invalid recurrence text is handled as degraded data rather than allowing a parsing error to take down the entire occurrence query: the original item is returned and the failure is logged.

those decisions are outside the recurrence grammar itself. so are permission checks, conflict validation between resources such as classes/people/environments, rules for all-day events and validation that an end date does not precede its start. the same merged calendar change touched those concerns and added tests around them.

that is the distinction I keep from this work: standards are useful because they give a shared representation, but they do not remove domain decisions. RRule can tell the system which dates belong to a recurrence. the application still has to decide what an occurrence means, how much expansion is safe, which timezone assumptions are valid, what conflicts are forbidden and what should happen when persisted rules are malformed.

those decisions are outside the recurrence grammar itself. so are permission checks, conflict validation between resources such as classes/people/environments, rules for all-day events and validation that an end date does not precede its start. the same merged calendar change touched those concerns and added tests around them.

that is the distinction I keep from this work: standards are useful because they give a shared representation, but they do not remove domain decisions. RRule can tell the system which dates belong to a recurrence. the application still has to decide what an occurrence means, how much expansion is safe, which timezone assumptions are valid, what conflicts are forbidden and what should happen when persisted rules are malformed.

writings.title: why Parcel treated pnpm packages as source code
writings.excerpt: a small 2021 resolver POC came from an assumption mismatch: Parcel used symlinks as a source-dependency signal, while pnpm used symlinks for normal installed packages.
writings.body:
the bug I was looking at in 2021 seemed like a package-resolution problem, but the useful explanation was one level below the failing import. Parcel 2 gave special treatment to dependencies it recognized as symbolic links because a symlink could mean that a package was local source code. pnpm, however, normally installs packages through links into its content-addressed store. the same filesystem fact therefore meant different things to the two tools.

the upstream Parcel issue was more useful than trying random bundler configuration. it documented the source-dependency behavior and discussion around pnpm's layout. once I could reproduce the assumption mismatch, the experiment became small: start from Parcel's resolver behavior, inspect the real path of a package and, when the resolved package came from `node_modules/.pnpm`, avoid treating the `source` marker as evidence that the dependency should receive source-package semantics.

that became `parcel-resolver-pnpm`, a proof-of-concept resolver. its implementation intentionally borrowed from Parcel's resolver internals and was tied to that period of Parcel 2, so I do not present it today as a maintained compatibility layer. the project page records the artifact; this note records the part I still find useful: two tools can both behave consistently with their own models and still fail when they assign different meaning to the same abstraction.

symlinks were not the root cause in isolation. the root cause was semantic: one side used 'is linked' to infer 'this is source', while the other used linking as its ordinary installation mechanism. reproducing that boundary gave me a much better debugging path than accumulating configuration until the symptom disappeared.

experiments.name: WebExtension RPC between page and content script
experiments.purpose: A collaborative 2023 Manifest V3 proof of concept for exposing request/response-style communication between page code and a browser extension content script through window.postMessage.
experiments.body:
This experiment explored a boundary that browser extensions make explicit: code injected into or running with the page does not have the same capabilities as the extension's content-script context. Instead of scattering event handling through both sides, the template models the communication as higher-level asynchronous actions such as `ping` or `sum`, transported through `window.postMessage`.

The repository is a small template/POC rather than a maintained RPC library. Its history also includes contributions from `legacybiel`, so I keep it explicitly framed as collaborative work rather than a solo library. It is relevant to the same broader line as AVA Pro — understanding the interfaces between browser contexts — while being a narrower experiment about the communication mechanism itself.

experiments.body: This belongs in the experiments collection rather than the project archive. It is a compact algorithm study from the period when C# was part of my formal programming work at IFRO, not a product or reusable library. featured_projects.name: Meu Caderno
featured_projects.purpose: an early-stage open-source local-first study application for organizing subjects, courses, learning projects, activities, grades, attendance, materials and accumulated knowledge without making a server mandatory.
featured_projects.body:
Meu Caderno is an early-stage personal project where product decisions and software architecture meet. the project is designed around offline-first use, user-owned local data, optional synchronization, progressive disclosure and avoiding lock-in. a project constitution makes those principles explicit, including reversibility, consent and limits around automated or AI-assisted behavior.

the current codebase is a Bun/Nx monorepo. the UI-independent core already contains typed domain models and Zod schemas for contexts, profiles, library, notebooks, activities and federation, alongside persistence/federation structures and adapters; the application is a Nuxt/Vue PWA designed to run without a mandatory backend. the delivery pipeline also reflects the same concern for control and verifiability, with GitHub Pages deployment, CodeQL, dependency automation, workflow linting/security checks and build attestations. the application is still at MVP/early-development stage, so this record remains hidden from the public project selection until the product surface is substantial enough to represent completed work rather than architectural direction.

this is not the first time local data and user control appeared in one of my projects. Ya Time Marker, a small PWA I published in 2021, already kept its usage history on the device and explicitly supported importing, exporting and deleting the user's data without collecting it centrally. I do not treat the two applications as one continuous architecture, but the older project makes the current local-first principles less disconnected from the rest of my history: the vocabulary became more deliberate; the concern itself is older.

featured_projects.body:
this project entry describes the artifact itself. AVA Pro packaged several Moodle-facing features into a web extension built around TypeScript/React: course navigation, course pinning, access/login helpers and chat/message flows that could be reached from the browser extension rather than only from the Moodle pages.

the repository is archival and I do not present it as an extension that should be installed against current Moodle/browser versions. the separate case study carries the more useful historical story: how the project moved my scraping experiments from static DOM extraction toward authenticated application flows, while this page remains the concise record of what was actually built.
